name: Luxor Temple
alternate_names: Ipet Resyt (ancient name, meaning 'the southern sanctuary')
category: Ancient Temple / UNESCO World Heritage Site

location.region: Upper Egypt (ancient Thebes, East Bank of the Nile, central Luxor city)

historical_description: Luxor Temple sits directly in the heart of modern Luxor city, on the east bank of the Nile. Unlike most Egyptian temples dedicated to a specific deity for eternal worship, Luxor Temple was largely dedicated to the rejuvenation of kingship, closely tied to the annual Opet Festival, during which statues of the Theban triad (Amun, Mut, and Khonsu) were ceremonially carried from Karnak to Luxor Temple to reaffirm the pharaoh's divine right to rule. The temple has been in continuous use in some form for over 3,400 years, later incorporating a Roman-era chapel, a mosque (Abu al-Haggag Mosque, still active today), and even earlier a Coptic church, layered atop the ancient structure.

construction_details.main_builders: Amenhotep III (18th Dynasty, primary construction circa 1400 BCE), with significant additions by Ramesses II (19th Dynasty) including the entrance pylon, courtyard, and colossal statues; a chapel added by Alexander the Great
construction_details.construction_period: circa 1400 BCE (Amenhotep III) with expansions through the Ptolemaic and Roman periods
construction_details.notable_features: First Pylon of Ramesses II, Colonnade of Amenhotep III, Court of Ramesses II, Court of Amenhotep III, obelisk (one of an original pair; its twin now stands in Place de la Concorde, Paris), colossal seated statues of Ramesses II
construction_details.layout: Oriented roughly north-south along the Nile, connected historically to Karnak Temple by the Avenue of Sphinxes

dynasty: 18th Dynasty (Amenhotep III) with major additions in the 19th Dynasty (Ramesses II), New Kingdom

opening_hours.daily_hours: 06:00–19:00 (approximate; often the last temple visited in the evening due to dramatic floodlighting)
opening_hours.notes: Luxor Temple is popular for evening visits when floodlights illuminate the columns and statues dramatically

ticket_price.notes: Prices are set by the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities and subject to periodic revision; confirm current rates via egymonuments.com or at the ticket office.

best_visiting_time.time_of_day: Evening, after sunset, when the temple is dramatically floodlit and daytime heat has subsided
best_visiting_time.season: October to April for milder daytime weather if visiting earlier in the day
best_visiting_time.note: Luxor Temple is one of the few major Egyptian sites where a nighttime visit is often considered superior to a daytime one

interesting_facts: One of Luxor Temple's original pair of obelisks was gifted to France in 1830 and now stands in the Place de la Concorde in Paris.
The Abu al-Haggag Mosque, built partly atop and within the ancient temple structure, remains an active place of worship today, illustrating over 3,000 years of continuous religious use at the site.
The temple was the ceremonial focus of the ancient Opet Festival, when Amun's statue was carried from Karnak to Luxor Temple by boat and in procession to symbolically renew the pharaoh's power.
Alexander the Great added a granite chapel within the temple, depicting himself in the traditional guise of an Egyptian pharaoh to legitimize his rule.
The temple's colonnade of Amenhotep III, with its towering papyrus-bud columns, is considered one of the finest examples of New Kingdom architecture.
Luxor Temple is uniquely located directly within a modern city center, with contemporary Luxor built up around and even over parts of the ancient site.
unesco_status: Part of UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Ancient Thebes with its Necropolis' (inscribed 1979)
accessibility_notes: Mostly paved, flat pathways within the temple courtyards, making it one of the more accessible ancient sites in Luxor, though some interior areas have uneven ancient stone flooring.
nearest_airport: Luxor International Airport (LXR), approx. 7 km away
